summary: Extends the HTTP Accept-Encoding header so a response can tell clients which content codings the server accepts in requests. Content codings such as gzip are common in responses but hard to discover for requests. It was replaced by RFC 9110.

eli5.summary: A server can tell you what kinds of squished packages it will accept from you. It was replaced by RFC 9110.

questions: how does a server advertise supported request content codings
how can clients compress http requests
how do servers advertise compression support for requests
subtitle: Letting servers tell clients which request compression methods they accept

tldr.problem: HTTP clients can compress request bodies to save bandwidth, but servers had no standardized way to advertise which compression methods they support in requests, unlike responses where Accept-Encoding is well established.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7694 extends the HTTP Accept-Encoding header field to work in responses as well as requests, allowing servers to declare which content codings (like gzip) they accept in request bodies, and recommends that 415 Unsupported Media Type responses include this header to help clients distinguish coding problems from other issues.
tldr.outcome: Clients can now discover supported request compression methods from server responses and error messages, making it easier to use compression in uploads and other request bodies. RFC 9110 supersedes this with consolidated HTTP semantics.

today: RFC 7694 is a Standards Track RFC published in November 2015. It was superseded by RFC 9110, which consolidated HTTP/1.1 semantics and core definitions into a single document.

sections.title: The Problem of Request Compression
sections.content:
In HTTP, content codings compress payload data for efficiency. The gzip content coding is extremely common in response bodies: a server compresses the HTML or JSON before sending it to the client, and the client decompresses it. This saves bandwidth.

Clients can also send compressed request bodies, for example when uploading large files or sending verbose data formats. But there was an asymmetry: when a server rejected a compressed request, it could not easily tell the client whether the problem was with the compression method itself or with something else (like the media type). And there was no standard way for a server to advertise that it supported compression in requests, the way HTTP response headers advertise server capabilities.
sections.eli5: Servers commonly tell clients 'here is the response compressed with gzip,' but they had no way to say 'I can also accept gzip-compressed requests from you.' When a client sent a compressed request and the server could not handle it, the client did not know why.

sections.title: Using Accept-Encoding in Responses
sections.content:
RFC 7694 says that the Accept-Encoding header field, normally used in HTTP requests, can also appear in responses. When present in a response, Accept-Encoding indicates what content codings the server was willing to accept in the associated request.

A response value of Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate tells the client that the server accepts gzip and deflate compression in requests. A response value of Accept-Encoding: identity (where identity means no encoding) tells the client that the server does not support any compression in requests. This information is specific to that resource and that request method; the same server might accept compression for other resources or other methods.
sections.eli5: A server can now include a header in its response saying 'I accept these compressed formats in requests.' If the client had tried an unsupported format, the header tells the client what to try next time.

sections.title: Practical Usage with Error Responses
sections.content:
The most common use case is when a client sends a request with a compression method the server does not support. The server responds with HTTP status 415 (Unsupported Media Type) and includes an Accept-Encoding header showing what it does support.

For example, a client sends a POST request using the compress content coding. The server does not support compress but does support gzip. It responds with status 415 and the header Accept-Encoding: gzip. The client then knows to retry the request using gzip instead. Alternatively, if the server does not support any compression in requests, it responds with Accept-Encoding: identity, making clear that the problem is the compression, not the media type or the request method.
sections.eli5: If a server says 'I do not accept that compression format,' it can include a helpful header: 'but I do accept these formats.' The client learns what to try next, without having to guess or ask a human.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.content:
For servers that do not support compression in requests at all, compliance is trivial: when a request uses a content coding and fails, respond with status 415 and the header Accept-Encoding: identity.

For servers that do support some compression methods, they must identify which methods are supported for each resource and method, and include the appropriate Accept-Encoding header in 415 responses when a request uses an unsupported compression method. Since the set of supported codings is usually static and small (often just gzip), adding the header is straightforward.

Servers can also use Accept-Encoding in successful responses to hint to clients that compression is supported, allowing clients to optimize future interactions with the resource.
sections.eli5: Servers that allow compressed uploads just need to include the Accept-Encoding header when they reject an unsupported compression method. It is a simple addition that makes clients much smarter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 7694 does not introduce new security risks; it only adds discovery and diagnostics for compression methods, which already exist in HTTP. However, better discoverability makes compression more commonly used, and compression in requests can be vulnerable to side-channel attacks such as BREACH when used over a secure channel.

BREACH is an attack that exploits compression to leak information from HTTPS responses; at the time of publication, it was unclear whether similar attacks apply to compression in HTTP requests. Implementers should be aware that enabling and advertising compression in requests might increase exposure to such attacks, though the attacks were not well characterized for requests.
sections.eli5: This RFC does not add new security problems, but it does make compression more common, which could be exploited in certain advanced attacks on encrypted connections. For ordinary uses, it is safe.
